main_text.p: XV. Dividitur & Finis, in finem per se, & per accidens; verum hæc divisio non caret vitiô : Finis per accidens appellatur vulgò, qui non intenditur, sed quem agens assequitur præter intentionem & propensionem naturæ: atqui quod præter intentionem agenti accidit, Finis aut causa finalis dici nequit; quia finis ideò & eatenus causa est, quia & quatenus movet efficientem, id est, quatenus ab efficiente intenditur: itaque cùm hoc sensu finis per accidens dicitur, Finis appellatione, non causa, sed effectum per accidens sive eventus intelligitur. Potest tamen divisio illa excusari, si per finem per se, intelligas finem, quem efficiens primò intendit; & per finem per accidens eum, quem intendit κατὰ [illegible, ~9 letters], id est, ut eo potiatur, si primo fine excidat.
main_text.head: THESIS I.
main_text.p: Subjectum est ἐκ τῶν πρός τι[?], denotatque respectum vel ad prædicatum, vel ad adjunctum: cum respectu ad prædicatum sumitur in doctrina de Enunciationes;

page.notes: The Greek phrase after "intendit" is blurred and not legible letter by letter; it is marked illegible. The Greek in the thesis paragraph ("ἐκ τῶν πρός τι") is read with doubt and marked [?]. The chapter title line is set in italic. The "THESIS I." label is treated as a level-2 heading. The page carries a rule ornament between the first paragraph and the chapter heading, and a faint stamp in the lower right corner, which is not transcribed. The printed "Enunciationes;" is kept as printed.
